entry.title: a post with marimo snippets
entry.content:
marimo notebooks can run Python directly in the reader’s browser. Opt a page in from its front matter:

---
layout: post
title: a post with marimo snippets
marimo: true
---

Nothing is loaded on pages without that flag, so bundling the plugin costs nothing site-wide.

Runnable snippets

Wrap fenced Python blocks in a container and the runtime turns them into an interactive notebook after the page loads:

import marimo as mo

slider = mo.ui.slider(1, 20, value=5, label="n")
slider

mo.md(f"The first {slider.value} squares: {[i**2 for i in range(1, slider.value + 1)]}")

Until the runtime has moved those blocks into place the container stays hidden, so readers never see the raw source flash before it becomes a notebook.

Embedding a hosted notebook

If you already publish a notebook — on marimo.app or your own WASM host — embed it instead:

{% al_marimo_embed src="https://marimo.app/l/your-notebook" height="700px" caption="Sampling demo" %}

The frame is sandboxed without allow-same-origin, so the embedded notebook cannot reach this page’s storage or cookies.

A note on what this loads

The marimo-snippets runtime is vendored into the plugin at a pinned version and served from your own site, rather than pulled from a CDN — so no third-party origin executes script in your readers’ pages. Running a notebook does contact marimo’s host, which is worth knowing before you opt a page in.

entry.content:
This is how a post with tabs looks like. Note that the tabs could be used for different purposes, not only for code.

First tabs

To add tabs, use the following syntax:

{% tabs group-name %}

{% tab group-name tab-name-1 %}

Content 1

{% endtab %}

{% tab group-name tab-name-2 %}

Content 2

{% endtab %}

{% endtabs %}

With this you can generate visualizations like:

  • php
  • js
  • ruby 
  • var_dump('hello');

  • console.log("hello");

  • pputs 'hello'

Another example

  • yaml
  • json 
  • hello:
  - "whatsup"
  - "hi"

  • {
  "hello": ["whatsup", "hi"]
}

Tabs for something else

  • text
  • quote
  • list

  • Regular text

entry.title: a post with pseudo code
entry.content:
This is an example post with some pseudo code rendered by pseudocode. The example presented here is the same as the one in the pseudocode.js documentation, with only one simple but important change: everytime you would use $, you should use $$ instead. Also, note that the pseudocode key in the front matter is set to true to enable the rendering of pseudo code. As an example, using this code:

```pseudocode
% This quicksort algorithm is extracted from Chapter 7, Introduction to Algorithms (3rd edition)
\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Quicksort}
\begin{algorithmic}
\PROCEDURE{Quicksort}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \IF{$$p < r$$}
        \STATE $$q = $$ \CALL{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, p, q - 1$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, q + 1, r$$}
    \ENDIF
\ENDPROCEDURE
\PROCEDURE{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \STATE $$x = A[r]$$
    \STATE $$i = p - 1$$
    \FOR{$$j = p$$ \TO $$r - 1$$}
        \IF{$$A[j] < x$$}
            \STATE $$i = i + 1$$
            \STATE exchange
            $$A[i]$$ with $$A[j]$$
        \ENDIF
        \STATE exchange $$A[i]$$ with $$A[r]$$
    \ENDFOR
\ENDPROCEDURE
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

Generates:

\begin{algorithm}

    \ENDIF
\ENDPROCEDURE

    \ENDFOR

entry.title: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning and its fundamentals

link.title: Introduction to Reinforcement Learning and its fundamentals

entry.content:
What is reinforcement learning? Have you played that game with a bouncy red ball, in which we have to make that ball reach the finish line but there are so many obstacles like a wall, or some needles which we have to skip to survive. If yes, then can you think of a way to teach a machine to play that game🤔?

The answer to the above question is Reinforcement learning. As the name suggests, you learn by reinforcing. Better yet, you learn by the mistakes you make and get rewarded for the correct steps you take.

Reinforcement Learning is the science an framework of learning and making decisions by interaction. Some examples of reinforcement learning problems are to teach a program:

  1. How to fly a helicopter.
  2. Manage an investment portfolio.
  3. Control a power Station.
  4. Make a robot walk.
  5. play video games(like the one I talked about in the beginning).

RL(short for Reinforcement Learning) is based on the reward hypothesis. Any goal can be formalized as the outcome of maximizing a cumulative reward. Thus for each of the above examples, we can stipulate a reward and apply the principles of RL.

Formalizing a RL problem requires to think about:

  1. time
  2. Consequences of actions.
  3. actively gather experience.
  4. predicting the future.
  5. dealing with uncertainity.

Formalizing the RL Problem

At each time step t, the agent:

  1. receives observation Oₜ (and reward Rₜ ).
  2. executes an action Aₜ.

The Environment, on the other hand:

  1. Receives the action Aₜ.
  2. emits observation Oₜ₊₁.

A reward is a scalar feedback that comes from the environment at each time-step and it helps the agent understand the impact of its action on the environment. This basically indicated the performance of the agent.

The agent’s job is to maximize the cumulative reward Gₜ = Rₜ + Rₜ₊₁ + Rₜ₊₂ + … . . It has only the future rewards and not the past rewards. The reason for this is, the rewards that have already been collected and observed, changing them will cause nothing good for us, that is why we only consider the future rewards. Basically the logic is that the future should be optimal from the current time-step. Sometimes Gₜ is also called return.

The expected cumulative reward from the state Sₜ=s is called the value v(s).

Value depends on the actions the agent takes. Goal is to maximize value by picking suitable actions. Rewards and values define utility of each states and action. There is no supervised feedback as in one type of reward is good and another type is bad. There is a recursive relation between cumulative reward Gₜ = Rₜ₊₁ + Gₜ₊₁. Therefore the value function can also be written as

NOTE: It is also possible to condition on actions along with the states in the above equation.

Policy defines the agent’s behaviour to a certain observation that it receives from the environment. It is a map from state to action. Policy can be deterministic like A = π(s) or Stochastic like π(A/s) = ℙ(A/s). Policy is also conditioned in the value equation to give the actual value function which is used as:

where γ is the discount factor ∈[0.0, 1.0] which essentially helps us weigh out the significance and importance of each reward. This is useful when we want to cater to long-term rewards instead of short term rewards or vice versa. Employing the recursive relation for Gₜ along with the discount factor, we can draw a recursive relation between the value functions which can be stated as

Here, Aₜ∼ π(s) means that action a = Aₜ is chosen by the policy π in state s. This is the Bellman Equation.

Now while creating RL agents, it is not always possible to find the ideal value functions which will give you the exact optimal value. To remove this barrier, we approximate the value functions. Even though in the presence of the exact value functions, the agent will behave optimally, but in the presence of approximated functions, it behaves well enough.

The last terminology we need to get familiar with is Model. Like a regular machine learning model, a RL model predicts what the environment will do next.

It either predicts the next state:

or it predicts the next(immediate) reward:

here, Ƿ(s, a, s’) is the probability of the next state being s’ given the present state is s and the action taken according to the policy is a. And ℛ(s, a) is the expected reward Rₜ₊₁ given the present state is s and the action taken according to the policy is a.

Phew!😵‍💫. This was a lot. It might seem overwhelming at first but try to find a connection between supervised machine learning algorithms and loss functions and Reinforcement Learning’s value functions and Policy. I hope this article gives you a good exposure to reinforcement learning.

See you later🐊

References

[1]. Key concepts on modern reinforcement learning, Ekaba Bisong.

[2]. DeepMind x UCL RL Lecture Series-Lecture 1.

entry.title: GraphGAN: Generative Adversarial Networks for Graphs

link.title: GraphGAN: Generative Adversarial Networks for Graphs

entry.content:
Before reading this article, you should know a little about Generative Adversarial Networks and Graph Datasets and Graph Representation Learning(not very much, just that nodes of a graph are fed into a neural network in the form of embeddings in a latent space of an arbitrary dimension D😉)

Now, Let’s jump onto the main topic of this article. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for Graphs.

But wait, generating graphs? Why?🤔. Generating text seems reasonable, generating images is understandable but graphs? Well, I thought this too, and the answer is very trivial. Graphs are just as important as texts or images. Let me give you an instance of where graphs are used for representing data. The protein sequence of a molecule is represented in the form of a graph network. Now imagine being able to generate protein molecules with absolutely new structures, that could cure cancer (okay, that is taking it a bit too far 😂) But really, think how easy it would become for researchers to produce new drugs if they could first get a vague idea of how the molecule should look, instead of experimenting again and again.

As we know, in a GAN architecture, the discriminator and the generator play a MinMax game between themselves. The generator learns from the gradient backpropagation of the discriminator loss and thus improves. Both generator and discriminator learn from each other and ultimately reach the equilibrium.

For graphs, the idea is the same, just the definitions and generator and discriminator change. Before going to the definitions, let’s define some terminologies so that you become comfortable with the rest of the mathematical concepts.

GraphGAN Framework

Let G = (V, E) be the given graph, where V = {v₁, …, vₙ } represents the set of vertices and E = {eₖₗ} where (i,j) goes from 1 to n represents the set of edges. For a given vertex νₙ, we define ℳ(νₙ) as the set of vertices directly connected to νₙ, the size of which is typically much smaller than the total number of vertices ν. We denote the underlying true connectivity distribution for vertex νₙas conditional probability Ť(ν|νₙ), which reflects νₙ connectivity preference distribution over all other vertices in V. From this point of view, ℳ(νₙ) can be seen as a set of observed samples drawn from Ť(ν|νₙ)

Generator

G(ν|νₙ; θg), which tries to approximate the underlying true connectivity distribution Ť(ν|νₙ), and generates (or selects, if more precise) the most likely vertices to be connected with νₙ from vertex set V.

Discriminator

D(ν, νₙ; θd), which aims to discriminate the connectivity for the vertex pair (ν, νₙ). D(v, vc; θd) outputs a single scalar representing the probability of an edge existing between ν and νₙ.

The optimal parameters of the generator and the discriminator can be learned by alternately maximizing and minimizing the value function V(G, D). In each iteration, discriminator D is trained with positive samples from Ť(ν|νₙ) (vertices in green) and negative samples from the generator G(ν|νₙ; θg) (vertices with blue stripes), and generator G is updated with policy gradient under the guidance of D. Competition between G and D drives both of them to improve their methods until G is indistinguishable from the true connectivity distribution. We discuss the implementation and optimization of D and G as follows.

Discriminator Optimization

the objective for the discriminator is to maximize the log probability of assigning the correct labels to both positive and negative samples, which could be solved by stochastic gradient ascent if D is differentiable with respect to θd. We define the discriminator as the sigmoid of the inner product of the node embeddings.

we need to update only dv and dνₙ by ascending the gradient with respect to them:

Generator Optmization

In contrast to the discriminator, the generator aims to minimize the log probability that the discriminator correctly assigns negative labels to the samples generated by G. In other words, the generator shifts its approximated connectivity distribution (through its parameters θG) to increase the scores of its generated samples, as judged by D. Because the sampling of v is discrete, we propose computing the gradient of V(G, D) with respect to θg by policy gradient:

A straightforward way is to define the generator as a softmax function over all other vertices. Softmax provides a concise and intuitive definition for the connectivity distribution in G, but it has two limitations in graph representation learning: 1) The calculation of softmax involves all vertices in the graph, which implies that for each generated sample ν, we need to calculate gradients ∇θg logG(ν|νₙ; θg) and update all vertices. This is computationally inefficient, especially for real-world, large-scale graphs with millions of vertices. 2) The graph structure encodes rich information of proximity among vertices, but Softmax completely ignores the utilization of structural information from graphs as it treats vertices without any discrimination. To address the aforementioned problems, in GraphGAN, we propose a new alternative to softmax for the generator called graph softmax.

We discuss graph softmax in detail as follows. To calculate the connectivity distribution G(ν|νₙ; θg), we first perform Breadth First Search (BFS) on the original graph G starting from vertex νₙ, which provides us with a BFS-tree Tₙ rooted at νₙ. Given Tₙ, we denote ℋₙ(ν) as the set of neighbours of ν (i.e., vertices that are directly connected to ν) in Tₙ, including its parent vertex and all child vertices if they exist. For a given vertex ν and one of its neighbours νₖ ∈ ℋₙ(ν), we define the relevance probability of νₖ given v as

Phew, a lot of maths and symbols 😬😶‍🌫️. But once you understand this, it’s pretty much over. All you need to know is if you know about GAN and its mathematics, it is mostly how well you can draw a parallel between it and GraphGAN. The sampling strategy for the generator is also dependent on the relevance probability of the nodes in the set ℋₙ(ν). I will not explain the details here because it is not that much important until you are actually trying to write your network. But I will give you an illustration through a diagram.

It’s basically choosing the next node which has the highest relevance probability🤷‍♂️. Makes sense.

Well, that is it. Everything is done. I hope you understand this. Took me 4 readings of the paper to understand it, so I understand that it is not easy. I have implemented the code myself and also added a few new things to stabilize the training like Wasserstein Loss instead of the regular loss(If you are reading this within 2 or 3 days of me writing this, then there are still a few commits that have to be made on my repository and as of now you won’t find the Wasserstein Loss implementation). I have attached the link to the official code and my personal implementation as well. Feel free to ask any doubts regarding this.

See You Later, 🐊.

You can display diff code by using the regular markdown syntax:

```diff
diff --git a/sample.js b/sample.js
index 0000001..0ddf2ba
--- a/sample.js
+++ b/sample.js
@@ -1 +1 @@
-console.log("Hello World!")
+console.log("Hello from Diff2Html!")
```

Which generates:

diff --git a/sample.js b/sample.js
index 0000001..0ddf2ba
--- a/sample.js
+++ b/sample.js
@@ -1 +1 @@
-console.log("Hello World!")
+console.log("Hello from Diff2Html!")

index 0000001..0ddf2ba
--- a/sample.js
+++ b/sample.js
@@ -1 +1 @@
-console.log("Hello World!")
+console.log("Hello from Diff2Html!")

@@ -98,6 +98,9 @@ The HTML output accepts a Javascript object with configuration. Possible options
   - `synchronisedScroll`: scroll both panes in side-by-side mode: `true` or `false`, default is `false`
